sections.h2: How an Ohio foreclosure ends in a sheriff sale
sections.html:
The lender sues in the county court of common pleas, wins a judgment, and the court orders the property sold. Under R.C. 2323.07 the court can order a tract sold whole or in parcels. When land spans several counties, it can direct the sheriff of each county, or a single officer, to make the sale. Chapter 2329 then governs how the sale runs.

Once you are served with the lawsuit, the home could be lost in three to six months. Open every piece of mail from the court, call your servicer right away, and stay in the house. Living there keeps the home in better shape, and the lender prefers it that way until the sheriff says otherwise.

Free help is a phone call away: Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, the Ohio Department of Commerce at 800-750-0750, Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446, and HUD approved counselors at 888-995-HOPE.

The sheriff summons three disinterested freeholders, who must live in the county and own real property there, to appraise the land by viewing it. For a residence, R.C. 2329.17 gives them twenty-one calendar days from the clerk's order to return a value. If they run past that window, they go unpaid, the appraised value becomes the auditor's latest value, and the sale proceeds. A court can approve a separate appraisal for good cause.

The municipality or township may also inspect any structures on the land before the sale. The sheriff's office can tell you whether an inspection has been set for your property.

The appraisal sets the floor for the first auction. Under R.C. 2329.20, land cannot sell for less than two-thirds of its appraised value, subject to exceptions in sections 2329.51 and 2329.52. A junior lienholder enforcing against land that carries a prior lien faces a modified minimum set by the court.

Two kinds of notice are needed. Under R.C. 2329.26, the creditor or its lawyer must serve written notice on the judgment debtor and every other party, and file it with proof of service at least seven calendar days ahead of the sale. A party in default for failing to appear need not be served. The officer must also advertise once a week for at least three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county.

The ad gives the date, time and place, or for an online sale the start date, minimum length and web address. It also states the required deposit and warns bidders that they answer for any costs, allowances and taxes the proceeds fall short of covering.

These rules have teeth. Under R.C. 2329.27, a sale made without the required notices is set aside on motion of an interested party. After the court confirms a sale, though, the order counts as a finding that notice was adequate and bars further motions to set the sale aside. If you spot a notice defect, raise it before confirmation.

Any bidder other than the foreclosing lender must put down a deposit tied to the home's appraised value. R.C. 2329.211 sets three tiers for residential property:

  • Two thousand dollars when the appraisal is ten thousand dollars or less.
  • Five thousand dollars when the appraisal is above ten thousand and up to two hundred thousand.
  • Ten thousand dollars when the appraisal is above two hundred thousand.

A purchaser who misses the deposit timing voids the sale, and the home may move to a provisional second sale if one was announced.

When a house in a residential mortgage foreclosure fails to sell at the first auction, R.C. 2329.52 calls for a second auction between seven and thirty days later. The highest bidder wins with no minimum bid, although costs, allowances and real estate taxes must still be covered. If the house is unsold after two auctions, it may be offered again without the minimum or disposed of another way the chapter allows.

Ohio sheriff sale sequence under Chapters 2323 and 2329
StageWhat happens
Order of saleCommon pleas court orders the foreclosed property sold
AppraisalThree freeholders, twenty-one days for a home
First auctionMinimum bid of two-thirds of appraised value
Public noticeWeekly for at least three consecutive weeks
Second auctionSeven to thirty days later, no minimum bid
ConfirmationWithin thirty days of the return of the writ
RedemptionAny time before confirmation

sections.h2: Redeeming or stopping an Ohio sheriff sale
sections.html:
You can redeem until the court confirms the sale. R.C. 2329.33 lets the debtor deposit with the clerk the judgment amount, all costs, and interest at eight percent a year on the purchase money from the day of sale. The court then sets the sale aside, applies the deposit to the judgment and awards the interest to the bidder. After confirmation, redemption under that section is over.

Timing is tight. Under R.C. 2329.31, the court reviews the sale and journalizes confirmation within thirty days of the return of the writ, though it may stay confirmation to let an owner redeem. The buyer then has thirty days after confirmation to pay the balance, and the officer records the deed within fourteen days after confirmation and payment. If the deed is late, the buyer can ask for a court order that works as the deed. The county auditor then updates ownership for tax purposes, and taxes that come due after the sale fall on the new owner.

Selling the house yourself can produce the redemption money. Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a written payoff, check the docket with the clerk, and keep the confirmation date in view. A cash buyer who can close before confirmation gives you a way to pay off the judgment and keep whatever equity remains.

Mediation is another route. A foreclosure case can be mediated anywhere from before filing up to confirmation of the sale, and it has even been done after the sheriff sale. Programs vary by county court, so call the court. After a sale, proceeds generally go in this order: the court, the sheriff, the county treasurer, then lienholders, with any remainder going to the owner. Beware firms that charge fees for services available for free. Save the Dream Ohio referrals cost nothing.

faqs.q: How long does a sheriff sale take after a foreclosure judgment in Ohio?
faqs.a: The statutes set pieces, not one total. Appraisal takes up to twenty-one days, advertising runs at least three weeks, confirmation follows within thirty days of the writ's return, and the buyer has thirty days to pay. The clerk can give you the dates on your case.

faqs.q: What is the minimum bid at an Ohio sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Two-thirds of the appraised value at the first auction. In a residential mortgage foreclosure, a second auction held seven to thirty days later has no minimum bid. Costs and real estate taxes still have to be covered.

faqs.q: Can I redeem my Ohio home after the sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Only before the court confirms the sale. You deposit the judgment amount, costs and eight percent interest on the purchase money with the clerk. Once confirmed, that right ends.

faqs.q: Do I have to move out before the Ohio sheriff sale?
faqs.a: No. Owners are urged to stay in the home and keep it in good condition until the sheriff says they must leave.

faqs.q: Where can I get free help with an Ohio foreclosure?
faqs.a: Call Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, or the Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446. HUD approved counselors are at 888-995-HOPE. Your county common pleas court can tell you whether it offers foreclosure mediation.
